o: Arises from the posterior divisions of L1–3

It arises from the posterior divisions of L2–4.
The obturator nerve takes the anterior divisions.
Lies inside the femoral sheath

It lies outside the sheath, lateral to it.
The sheath contains artery, vein and the femoral canal.
Supplies adductor longus

Adductor longus is supplied by the obturator nerve.
The femoral supplies quadriceps, sartorius, pectineus and iliacus.
Has the saphenous nerve as its longest branch

The saphenous nerve runs in the adductor canal and down to the medial foot.
It is purely sensory.
Arises from the anterior divisions of L2–4

It forms within psoas and emerges at its medial border.
It runs on the side wall of the pelvis.
Always supplies pectineus

Pectineus is usually supplied by the femoral nerve.
The obturator (or accessory obturator) helps only sometimes.
Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen

It leaves through the obturator canal.
The sciatic nerve uses the greater sciatic foramen.
Supplies the skin of the lateral thigh

It supplies skin on the medial thigh.
The lateral thigh is supplied by the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
Leaves the pelvis above piriformis

It usually leaves below piriformis.
The superior gluteal nerve leaves above.
Supplies the hamstrings through its tibial part

Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, long head of biceps and the hamstring part of adductor magnus.
These are all tibial-part muscles.
Supplies the short head of biceps through its tibial part

The short head is supplied by the common peroneal part.
It is the only thigh muscle with that supply.
Usually divides at the apex of the popliteal fossa

It usually divides into tibial and common peroneal there.
A high division in the pelvis is common.
Comes from L2 and L3

It comes from the posterior divisions of L2 and L3.
It emerges at the lateral border of psoas.
Passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the ASIS

It enters the thigh close to the anterior superior iliac spine.
Its course is variable.
Causes meralgia paraesthetica when compressed

Compression gives numbness and burning over the lateral thigh.
There is no weakness, as it is purely sensory.
Can pass through a tunnel 1 cm medial to the ASIS

It may be held in iliac fascia for about 3 cm above the inguinal ligament.
These sites explain its entrapment. (Last's p. 146, 214, 363)
Leaves the pelvis below piriformis

It leaves above piriformis with the superior gluteal vessels.
It is the only nerve to do so.
Supplies gluteus maximus

Gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve.
The superior gluteal supplies medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae.
When cut, makes the pelvis drop on the same side when standing on that leg

Standing on the weak side, the pelvis drops on the opposite side (positive Trendelenburg).
Medius and minimus can no longer hold the pelvis level.
Supplies tensor fasciae latae

It ends in tensor fasciae latae.
This muscle also helps hold the pelvis level.
Supplies all the muscles of the back of the leg

It supplies the superficial and deep calf muscles.
These are the plantarflexors and toe flexors.
Runs with the anterior tibial artery

It runs with the posterior tibial artery.
The deep peroneal nerve runs with the anterior tibial.
Ends by dividing into deep and superficial peroneal nerves

It ends as the medial and lateral plantar nerves.
The common peroneal divides into deep and superficial peroneal.
Passes in front of the medial malleolus

It passes behind the medial malleolus, under the flexor retinaculum.
This is the tarsal tunnel.
Supplies peroneus longus

Peroneus longus and brevis are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve.
The deep peroneal supplies the anterior compartment.
Supplies the skin of most of the dorsum of the foot

Most of the dorsum is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve.
The deep peroneal supplies only the first web space.
Lies superficial to the extensor retinaculum

It passes deep to the retinaculum with the anterior tibial artery.
The superficial peroneal lies superficial.
Supplies the skin of the first web space

This small area is the test for a deep peroneal lesion.
It also supplies extensor digitorum brevis.
The femoral vein lies lateral to the artery

From lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, canal (NAVY).
The vein is medial.
The femoral canal contains a lymph node

The canal contains fat, lymphatics and a lymph node (of Cloquet).
It is the site of femoral hernia.
The femoral nerve lies within the femoral sheath

The nerve lies outside the sheath, lateral to it.
The sheath is a downward extension of abdominal fascia.
The femoral sheath is formed from transversalis and iliac fascia

The front is transversalis fascia, the back iliac fascia.
It encloses artery, vein and canal.
Is formed within psoas major

It forms within the substance of psoas.
Its branches emerge from the lateral and medial borders and the front of the muscle.
Gives the iliohypogastric nerve from L2

Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal come from L1.
Genitofemoral comes from L1 and L2.
Gives the femoral nerve from its anterior divisions

The femoral comes from the posterior divisions of L2–4.
The obturator comes from the anterior divisions.
Gives a genitofemoral nerve that emerges from the lateral border of psoas

Genitofemoral emerges on the front of psoas.
It is the only nerve to pierce the front of the muscle.

questions.s: Segmental supply in the lower limb:
o: The ankle jerk is S1

The ankle jerk tests S1 (and S2).
It is lost with an S1 root lesion.
The knee jerk is L3 and L4

The knee jerk tests L3 and L4 through the femoral nerve.
It is lost with an L4 root lesion.
Hip flexion is L2 and L3

Hip flexion is mainly L2 and L3.
Hip extension is L4 and L5.
Ankle dorsiflexion is L4 and L5

Dorsiflexion is L4 and L5; plantarflexion S1 and S2.
So an L5 lesion can give foot drop.
